title: Acids, bases and the two arrows

steps.text: An **acid** gives up H⁺; a **base** uses a lone pair to take it. Every proton transfer is two curved arrows: (1) from the base's lone pair to the H, and (2) from the H–A bond onto A. The arrows always start at electrons, never at the proton.
Hydroxide's lone pair grabs the O–H proton, and the O–H bond's electrons stay behind on oxygen as acetate.

**Lower pKa = stronger acid.** Compare the acid on each side: the equilibrium favours the **weaker acid** (higher pKa). Stronger acid + stronger base → weaker acid + weaker base; each pKa unit is a factor of 10. Anchors: HCl −7, RCOOH 5, H2CO3 6.4, phenol 10, H2O 15.7, ROH 16, RC≡CH 25, NH3 38, alkane 50.
The first arrow (amide lone pair to the H) is drawn. Add the arrow that leaves the electrons on carbon.
Ethanol is mixed with NaHCO3. Which way does the equilibrium lie?

options.text: Left: ethanol stays ethanol, because carbonic acid (pKa 6.4) is a much stronger acid than ethanol (pKa 16).
options.explains: Right. The equilibrium favours the weaker acid, and here that is ethanol on the left. Bicarbonate is far too weak a base.

options.text: Right: bicarbonate is a base, so it deprotonates any O–H.
options.explains: Being a base isn't enough; it has to be a stronger base than the one it would form. Ethoxide (from pKa 16) is much stronger than bicarbonate (from pKa 6.4).

options.text: Right, because CO2 bubbles off and pulls the reaction over.
options.explains: CO2 only forms if carbonic acid forms, and with ethanol almost none does. The fizz is a sign of a carboxylic acid, not an alcohol.

options.text: Right: bicarbonate removes a C–H proton from ethanol.
options.explains: C–H bonds in ethanol (pKa about 50) are even less acidic than the O–H. Bicarbonate can't touch them.

steps.text: Why do acids differ? Look at the **conjugate base**: the more stable its negative charge, the stronger the acid. Check, in order: the **atom** carrying the charge (bigger down a group, more electronegative across a row), **resonance** spreading it, **induction** from nearby electronegative atoms, and the **orbital** (sp > sp2 > sp3).
Acetic acid (pKa 4.8) is about 10^11 times more acidic than ethanol (pKa 16). What is the main reason?

options.text: In acetate the negative charge is shared by two oxygens through resonance; in ethoxide it sits on one oxygen.
options.explains: Right. Resonance stabilization of the conjugate base is the big effect. The electron-withdrawing C=O adds a smaller inductive push.

options.text: The charge in acetate is on a different, more electronegative atom.
options.explains: The charge is on oxygen in both acetate and ethoxide, so the atom isn't the difference.

options.text: Acetic acid has more O–H bonds to give up.
options.explains: Each molecule has one O–H. Acidity is about how stable the anion is, not how many H atoms there are.

options.text: The carbanion of acetic acid is stabilized by the C=O.
options.explains: The proton that leaves is on oxygen, not carbon. Acetic acid's C–H bonds (pKa about 25) are not what makes it acidic.

steps.text: Tap the atom that loses its proton first when one equivalent of NaNH2 is added.
steps.explain: The O–H (pKa about 16) is far more acidic than the alkyne C–H (pKa 25), so the base takes the O–H proton first. Charge on electronegative oxygen beats the sp-carbon effect.

steps.text: You shake an unknown with aqueous NaHCO3 and it fizzes. Which compound could it be?

options.explains: Right. A carboxylic acid is stronger than carbonic acid (pKa 6.4), so bicarbonate deprotonates it and the carbonic acid formed falls apart into CO2.
Phenol dissolves in NaOH but not NaHCO3: it is a weaker acid than carbonic acid (pKa 6.4), so the equilibrium lies left and no CO2 forms.
Alcohols are much weaker acids than carbonic acid; bicarbonate doesn't deprotonate them.
Benzaldehyde has no acidic O–H at all, so there is nothing for bicarbonate to remove.

steps.text: Now the alcohol is the base. Draw both arrows.
